anchors.fact: Hawaiians traditionally roasted the big ti stems underground for several days, as agave is roasted in Mexico; roasting turns the starch to sugar (Oxford OKOLEHAO, pdf 1419; Alexander 1891 p. 157 describes the baking). F4
anchors.meaning: The skill and the plant were the islands' own before any still: comes first in the telling (Wren). **Never** the traditional ti "beer" (C1: Alexander p. 87 says Hawaiians used neither fermented nor distilled drink).

anchors.fact: Oxford: a still "jury-rigged" from "two discarded whaling ship blubber-boiling pots, with a gun barrel to draw off the spirit" (pdf 1419). Alexander 1891 p. 157, the earliest account: iron pots "procured from ships", a gun barrel as the tube. F5, F6
anchors.meaning: Cooking pots and a gun barrel doing a still's job: the wrong parts that worked. Pots and gun barrel on two sources; "discarded" and "whaling" are Oxford's alone (C3), so say them as Oxford tells it or leave them.
anchors.speaksTo: can fix anything, with whatever's to hand

anchors.fact: Oxford: William Stevenson, 1790s (pdf 1419). Alexander: distilling "is said to have been first practiced here by" him, "before the year 1800" (p. 157). F2, F3
anchors.meaning: Name him plainly, once, as the man the story credits ("the man usually credited"). Never "fugitive", "convict", "Australian". The guest isn't him: the fix, not the maker, is the point.

anchors.fact: *okole* = "bottom", *hao* = "iron" (Oxford pdf 1419). Why: Oxford, the twin pots looked like buttocks; Rowley 2014, they "were said to" and the nickname "stuck". F7
anchors.meaning: The bodge's own joke became the spirit's name: the mark it left. Meaning of the word is fact; the reason is "the story goes". "The name is Hawaiian", never "the Hawaiians named it". "Bottom" once, warmly.

anchors.fact: "At one time almost every chief had his still" (Alexander 1891 p. 157). F8
anchors.meaning: The makeshift wasn't a one-off: it was copied and kept. **Chiefs, not ordinary people**, and no date. Wren's limb 3 ("ordinary people used it for a long time") has no page for the still itself: what lasted on the record is the spirit and the name.

anchors.fact: Local Hawaiian distilleries make okolehao again from ti root with sugar cane (Oxford pdf 1421); Island Distillers' 100-proof cane-and-ti (Rowley 2014). F10
anchors.meaning: Made **again**, never "still": production broke off (pdf 1421, "only since 2012 … again"). The thing is kept, not replaced. Present tense on 2014/2021 sources; **no year** (C2); bottle availability is Tomás's to check.
anchors.speaksTo: "don't worry, we'll just get a new one" answered

anchors.fact: Oxford: the ti "is a relative of the agave", its stems roasted underground "as is done with agave piñas in Mexico" (OKOLEHAO pdf 1419); traditionally, mezcal piñas are roasted "in a conical earthen or stone-lined pit underground for several days" (MEZCALEROS pdf 1287). Joven mezcal is unaged (MEZCALEROS pdf 1290; *Codex* p. 165, "young"). F4
anchors.meaning: Why mezcal: the nearest relative, traditionally roasted the same way. **"Traditionally" stays** (R10): not every mezcal is pit-roasted today. **Never called okolehao** (Wren). Say "joven mezcal", never "joven" alone: a "joven" tequila can be a caramel-coloured gold (Oxford SAUZA pdf 1743). The bottle is a stand-in, so nothing about it is "his" or "theirs".
anchors.speaksTo: makeable from an ordinary kitchen; with what's to hand

anchors.fact: A label reading okolehao doesn't promise ti: the 1960s Hawaiian Distillers' was bourbon with ti extract (Oxford pdf 1421); in 2026 an attorney estimated nine label applications since 2015, "several" described as rums (Aloha State Daily, 24 Feb 2026, secondary). F11, F12
anchors.meaning: The dossier's reason the glass makes do. Guest text needn't say it; if it does, "a bottle by that name may not be what the story made".

anchors.fact: Oxford: marmalade "includes tangible pieces of peel" and "simultaneously provides sweetness and flavor" (MARMALADE AND JAM pdf 1240). *Codex* p. 77: a teaspoon of orange marmalade in Alex Day's Little Victory (2013) brings "a touch of sweetness and a pleasant bitterness".
anchors.meaning: Sweetness is on both pages; **the bitterness is the *Codex*'s, said of one drink.** "Does the bitters' job" is our reading, not a book's.

cocktail.closingLine: Strain it through the gap in the lid. Then leave the jar by the sink, and enjoy a room where nothing's broken.
method: Take a clean jar with a screw lid (about 350 to 500 ml). A marmalade jar that's nearly finished is best: leave about 1½ teaspoons in it and scrape the sides down. Otherwise, spoon the marmalade into any clean jar.
Pour in the mezcal. Stir with the spoon for about 20 seconds, scraping the bottom, until the marmalade has loosened into the spirit.
Fill the jar two-thirds with ice. Screw the lid on tight and shake hard for about 10 seconds, until the jar is too cold to hold comfortably.

Put the large cube in a small tumbler. Loosen the lid a quarter turn, hold it in place with your thumb and strain it through the gap: the lid holds the ice back. A few shreds of peel will come through. Leave them in.
cocktail.name: Good for Years

recipe.note: any joven mezcal from 40% to 50%; an espadín is the easiest to find
an ordinary one, not reduced-sugar: the sugar and a bitter edge in one spoon

cocktail.tagline: Everyone says get a new one. You've already got the back off.

reading.epigraph: No shaker, no strainer, no syrup. Just the last of a jar.
whoYouAre: Someone's lamp has died, or the zip's gone on a coat, and they're already saying it's had its day. You've got the back off before they've finished the sentence. A hair grip, a folded bit of card, tape from the kitchen drawer: you use whatever's there, and it works. It looks a bit odd. It lasts for years.

Quieter, though, is this. At a party where nothing's broken, you're not quite sure where to stand, and a dripping tap in the kitchen feels like being let in. What gets to you is the shrug, and "just get a new one", because a world that throws things away has less room for you in it. When you mend something, people keep their own thing, the bike they learned on or a grandparent's lamp, and the piece of their life that comes with it. And you show them what was wrong, so the impossible turns out to be ordinary.
yours: In Hawaii, people had long known how to bring the sweetness out of the ti plant, a relative of the agave: they roasted its big stems underground for days. Then, before 1800, distilling arrived, and the man usually credited with it is William Stevenson. His still was a makeshift: iron pots off the ships, with a gun barrel to carry the vapour.

It caught on. One history from 1891 says that at one time almost every chief had a still. And the contraption left its mark on the name. The spirit is called okolehao, which is Hawaiian: *okole* means bottom, and *hao* means iron. The pots were said to look like one, and the nickname stuck. Distillers on the islands make it from ti root again today.

I like to think that's the best ending a makeshift can have: people copied it, made a joke of its looks, and named the whole thing after it. Your repairs go the same way. All over the place, things are still working because of you, held together with something they were never meant to have, and someone smiles at the tape every time they use them. They're smiling because the thing is still theirs.

The cocktail I've made for you isn't okolehao. A true one is hard to find outside Hawaii, and not every bottle with that name on it has been made from ti root. So I made do, as a nod to that still. It's a mezcal Old-Fashioned, the cocktail at its most classic: a spirit, a little sugar, something bitter. Mezcal's agave is traditionally roasted underground for days, just as the ti was. There's no syrup and no bottle of bitters: a spoonful of orange marmalade does both jobs, sweet from the sugar and bitter from the peel. And it's best shaken in the marmalade jar itself, the nearly finished one that was on its way to the recycling, then poured through the gap under the loosened lid. The jar is the shaker and the strainer. It comes out soft orange and a little smoky, with a bitter edge and a few shreds of peel.

Next time you're asked round and nothing's broken, leave the dripping tap alone. Stay in the room with everyone else; the tap can wait. They didn't invite you for what you can mend. They invited you because they like having you there. And for once, you can enjoy the evening too.
